newsitem.title: USA: Rockwell's profits lower due to charges.
newsitem.headline: Rockwell's profits lower due to charges.

text.p: Rockwell International Corp. Wednesday reported sharply lower profits for the latest quarter due to one-time acquisition and restructuring charges.

Rockwell, which manufactures a variety of electronic and automotive components, earned $97 million, or 45 cents a share, in its fiscal fourth quarter ended in September, down from $189 million, or 88 cents a share in the year-ago period.

The quarter's results included one-time charges of $74 million for restructuring and $121 million related to its acquisition of Brooktree Corp., and a one-time gain of $76 million from settlements of income tax and insurance claims.

Earnings from continuing operations increased 67 percent to $192 million, or 88 cents a share, from $115 million, or 53 cents a share. Revenues grew to $2.66 billion from $2.49 billion, helped by a 12 percent growth in electronics sales.
Rockwell, which has been moving away from its traditional reliance on the defence industry to high-tech electronics, said it expects continued growth in the coming year.

"We have set an objective of increasing our sights on earnings growth up to 15 percent," Chairman Donald Beall said in an interview. "It used to be in the low double-digits. Our growth will be driven by our electronics businesses."

The company's Semiconductor Systems business, which had fourth quarter earnings 55 percent above the year-ago period, is expected to maintain its 1996 earnings momentum, Beall said. The unit makes personal computer and fax modem chipsets.
Beall added that a strong commercial air transport market will allow earnings growth for avionics and communications while its automation and automotive units are also seen growing in 1997.
The pending sale of its aerospace and defence businesses to Boeing Co. will also contribute to meeting earnings targets and will position Rockwell for acquisitions, Beall said.
"We are looking at external and internal investments in all of these businesses but I'm not forecasting anything," he said.
Beall said Rockwell has no plans at the moment for any other major divestitures or sale of assets.

With the pending sale of its aerospace and defence businesses to Boeing, Rockwell seems to be nearing the end of a transformation from a defence company working for government dollars to a diversified commercial enterprise.

Federal funds account for just 6 percent of revenues compared with 63 percent in 1984. Electronics, which now accounts for 70 percent of sales, is viewed by Beall as the jewel in the crown of the new-look Rockwell.
Beall said he would continue to raise value for shareholders in the coming year. The company previously said it plans to repurchase $1 billion of its stock.
Rockwell rose $2.25 to $57.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
